hints: Each child only compares with the child on the left and the child on the right. Can you satisfy the 'left neighbour' rule and the 'right neighbour' rule separately?

Two passes: left-to-right gives each child 1 + left neighbour's count if their score is higher; right-to-left does the same against the right neighbour. Each child's final count is the max of the two.

1. left[i] = 1 for all; for i = 1..n−1, if scores[i] > scores[i−1], left[i] = left[i−1] + 1.
  2. Walk from the right with a running value: right = 1, raise it when scores[i] > scores[i+1], else reset to 1.
  3. Add max(left[i], right) to the total.
  4. Return the total.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Start everyone at 1 and keep sweeping, fixing any child who should have more than a neighbour, until nothing changes.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Two greedy passes (left rule, right rule) and take the max per child.

explain: Sample 1 is [3,1,4]. Left pass: [1,1,2] (4 > 1). Right pass: [2,1,1] (3 > 1). Max per child: [2,1,2], total 5. In sample 2 [2,5,5,1], equal neighbours need no ordering, so we get [1,2,2,1] = 6. Taking the max keeps both rules true and is the smallest value that does, so the total is minimal. Remember the rule is only for STRICTLY higher scores.
recognize: Each element must beat its neighbours when it is larger, with the minimum total → two passes (left rule, right rule) and take the max.
